extra.message: Self-assigned admin role at registration — Any anonymous user can register as marketplace_admin and gain unrestricted access to all admin-only endpoints, user data, orders, payouts, and system configuration [verified: Register endpoint at auth.py:24-27 initializes role=UserRole.BUYER but immediately overwrites it with UserRole(data.role) for any role value in the UserRole enum including marketplace_admin, with no authorization check — an anonymous attacker can self-assign admin and bypass all require_role([MARKETPLACE_ADMIN]) guards used across the codebase.]

Hardcoded weak default SECRET_KEY for JWT signing — Complete bypass of authentication - attacker can forge JWT tokens for any user including marketplace_admin, gaining full access to all protected endpoints [verified: SECRET_KEY defaults to 'your-secret-key-change-in-production' on config.py:6, used directly in security.py:22 to sign HS256 JWTs; pydantic-settings reads from .env/env, but no .env or .env.example exists in the repo, so any deployment that fails to set the env var inherits this well-known default — an attacker can forge valid tokens for any user including marketplace_admin.]

Weak default SECRET_KEY for JWT signing — Attackers who discover the default SECRET_KEY can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, including marketplace_admin, gaining full system access. [verified: Same hardcoded default SECRET_KEY on config.py:7 as finding [0] — the weak default flows to jwt.encode/decode in security.py with no compensating control; no .env file, env.example, or deployment config ensures an override, making JWT forgery trivial if the default is used in production.]

Self-assigned admin role via registration — Any unauthenticated user can register as marketplace_admin and gain full administrative access to the platform including user management, moderation, payouts, audit logs, and all sensitive data. [verified: The RegisterRequest schema accepts role as an unconstrained plain str defaulting to 'buyer', and the registration endpoint (auth.py:18-20) explicitly allows any role value present in the UserRole enum—including 'marketplace_admin'—with no further guard; an unauthenticated attacker can send POST /api/auth/register with {"role":"marketplace_admin"} to gain full admin access.]

OS Command Injection via ping host parameter — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the application process [verified: User-controlled `host` query parameter is concatenated directly into `_os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` at line 118 with zero sanitization; the `_wrk_gate` provides only authentication, not input validation, and the host parameter is not a trusted input per the threat model.]

All uploaded files publicly accessible via StaticFiles mount — Unauthenticated access to sensitive uploaded files including vendor documents, dispute evidence, and private uploads that should be access-controlled [verified: StaticFiles mount at /uploaded_files serves all files (including dispute_evidence and vendor_document) without auth, bypassing the category-based access controls in /api/files/{id}/download. Additionally, GET /api/files/{id} returns stored_filename and category to any authenticated user with zero ownership check, enabling trivial enumeration of all file URLs for unauthenticated download.]

Path traversal arbitrary file write via ref parameter — Arbitrary file write to any location on the filesystem accessible to the process, including overwriting critical system files or planting malicious content [verified: User-controlled `ref` parameter from query params or JSON body is used directly in `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f"{ref}.json"` at line 60 with no path sanitization, enabling traversal (e.g., `../../etc/passwd`).]

NoSQL Injection via unsanitized MongoDB query — Unauthorized data access from MongoDB, potential enumeration of all records, and possible remote code execution via $where JavaScript injection. [verified: Duplicate of finding 3: user-supplied JSON body is passed directly to MongoDB `find_one()` at line 133 with no operator filtering or validation.]

Path traversal via uncontrolled filename in file write — Arbitrary file write outside the intended directory, potentially leading to code execution or system compromise. [verified: Duplicate of finding 9: user-controlled `name` parameter is used unsanitized in `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` at line 139 for arbitrary file writes.]

XXE via XML parser with external entity resolution — Arbitrary file read on the server, SSRF to internal services, and denial of service via entity expansion attacks. [verified: Duplicate of finding 1: `etree.XMLParser(load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False)` at line 147 parses user-supplied XML with external entity resolution fully enabled.]

File type validation bypass via spoofed Content-Type header — Attackers can upload malicious files (e.g., HTML with embedded JavaScript, executable scripts) by providing a whitelisted Content-Type while sending different file content [verified: save_upload_file validates only client-supplied Content-Type (line 24), not actual file content — no magic-bytes check exists. File extension comes from attacker-controlled filename (line 33) with no extension allowlist, and StaticFiles serves by extension (main.py:27), enabling stored XSS via HTML upload with spoofed Content-Type.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Attackers can conduct unlimited brute-force password guessing attacks and account enumeration without any throttling or lockout. [verified: Same absence of rate limiting as finding [3]; the login at auth.py:34 and register at auth.py:16 endpoints lack any IP-based lockout, CAPTCHA, or throttling, permitting automated brute-force and mass account creation.]

JWT cookie missing Secure flag — JWT access token cookie transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, enabling session hijacking via network interception [verified: Login endpoint at auth.py:49 sets the JWT cookie with httponly=True and samesite='lax' but omits secure=True; no HTTPS enforcement or HSTS is visible in the application, so the token cookie can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP if deployed without TLS termination.]

CSV formula injection in data exports — When an admin opens exported CSV files in spreadsheet applications, malicious formulas injected into user-controlled fields can execute, potentially leading to command execution on the admin's machine or data exfiltration. [verified: Same vulnerability as finding 0: attacker-supplied text in orders/vendors/products/disputes flows unsanitized through csv.writer() in all four export endpoints; Pydantic schemas impose no constraint on leading = + - @ characters and no output escaping is applied.]

CSV formula injection in data exports — When an admin opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, injected formulas can exfiltrate data to attacker-controlled servers or execute local commands [verified: User-controlled fields (shipping_name, shipping_address, buyer email, business_name, dispute reason/description, product name) pass through Pydantic str schemas with no formula-character validation and are written to CSV via csv.writer() without sanitization — no regex validator, no cell-prefix escaping, no middleware filtering exists anywhere.]

Reflected XSS via HTML string concatenation — Reflected cross-site scripting allowing execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of an ops user viewing a crafted URL [verified: User-controlled `copyline` query parameter is concatenated into an HTML string via `"

" + copyline + "

..."` at line 26 with no escaping, yielding reflected XSS in the `HTMLResponse`.]

JWT/ops token leak and log injection in ops endpoint — Exposure of JWT access tokens and internal ops tokens through log files accessible to operators, developers, or log aggregation systems; log injection can forge log entries or corrupt log analysis [verified: `logger.warning("ops tally body=%s bearer=%s", body, request.headers.get("authorization"))` at line 52 writes the raw request body and Authorization header to logs with no redaction, exposing JWT/ops tokens to log consumers.]

Sensitive data exposure in logs (Authorization header and request body) — JWT access tokens and sensitive request payloads are written to application logs, enabling credential theft and account takeover if logs are compromised. [verified: Duplicate of finding 5: raw body and Authorization header are logged verbatim at line 52 with no token redaction or sanitization.]

Server-Side Template Injection / XSS via Jinja2 |safe filter — Cross-site scripting (XSS) allowing session theft, credential phishing, or arbitrary JavaScript execution in the context of the operations dashboard [verified: User-controlled `card` query parameter is rendered via `Template("{{ card|safe }}").render(card=card)` at line 81 with the `|safe` filter disabling auto-escaping, yielding reflected XSS; the ops gate authenticates but does not sanitize.]

CORS origin reflection with credentials — Any origin can make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint, enabling data theft from authenticated users via malicious websites. [verified: Duplicate of finding 6: Origin header reflected into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` at line 97.]

JWT access token stored in localStorage vulnerable to XSS exfiltration — An attacker exploiting any XSS on the frontend can steal the JWT token from localStorage and impersonate the victim, gaining full access to their account including PII, orders, and payment data. [verified: AuthContext.jsx stores the JWT access token in localStorage at lines 35/44, directly undermining the backend's httpOnly cookie protection (auth.py line 54: httponly=True). The token is accessible to any JavaScript executing on the page; with no CSP headers configured anywhere in the frontend, any future XSS on any page would immediately expose the JWT for exfiltration, enabling full account takeov]

Hardcoded demo credentials exposed in login page — Any attacker visiting the login page can use the displayed credentials to log in as admin, vendor, support, or buyer, gaining unauthorized access to the application. [verified: Login.jsx:45-51 unconditionally displays demo admin/vendor/support/buyer credentials to every page visitor with no environment guard, and seed.py:50-53 creates those exact accounts with is_verified=True and elevated roles (including MARKETPLACE_ADMIN) with no production guard; if seed.py is ever run against a production database, any visitor can log in with full admin privileges.]

User enumeration via registration error messages — An attacker can build a list of valid user email addresses for targeted phishing, credential stuffing, or further attacks [verified: Registration at auth.py:20 returns distinct HTTP 400 'Email already registered' vs success/other validation errors, with no generic masking — an attacker can probe emails to build a list of registered users.]

Internal file path disclosure in upload API response — Reveals server filesystem structure to API consumers, facilitating targeted path traversal and filesystem-based attacks [verified: POST /api/files/upload returns FileUploadOut.from_orm(file_record) which includes file_path set via os.path.join(settings.UPLOAD_DIR, category, uuid) — exposing the server's upload directory structure in every upload response. The developers intentionally omitted file_path from FileRecordOut (GET endpoint), confirming this disclosure in the upload response is unintended.]

Security headers deliberately disabled in ops endpoint — Browsers rendering responses from this endpoint will have XSS audit filtering disabled and no CSP enforcement, increasing the impact of any HTML/JS injection vulnerabilities [verified: The response at line 104 explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and `Content-Security-Policy: ""`, disabling browser security controls; the response is JSON so practical impact is low but the misconfiguration is present on a reachable endpoint.]
